Foster’s Name: Pamela Lee
General Personality: playful, well behaved, likes dogs, chases cats. knows sit very well. calm except when first greeting a person. Can be exuberant when first greeting a family member. We are working on this with treats when maintaining a sitting position rather than jumping. I suspect she may have been hit/beaten in the past. i have to get her to lay down before I can pet her or give belly rubs.
Daily Routine: sits near me or plays with other dog in the house. Chews on Kong if treats are in it, plays in the back, fenced in yard.
Food: dog chow
Ideal Family & Home for foster dog: has another dogs, no cats. Has older children. Has a fenced yard or can walk her. Willing to give attention with treats. willing to continue training on no jumping when greeting people.
Houstrained? (Scale 1-5): 5
Does your foster use a kennel without excessive barking/whining, escape attempts or destruction?: some whining. She is not desrtuctive when I leave her alone to go out or when I go to bed. I have only had to use a kennel/crate when she first came to me.
Where do they sleep at night?: downstairs in the livingroom on her blanket
Do they sleep through the night?: Yes
Kid exposure: my grandchildren, ages 9 and 6. she likes them and they liked her. played fetch in the back yard with them. It went well after she settled from greeting them. She might knock younger children down until she is fully trained on polite greeting.
Cat exposure: barkes and wants to chase my cats. she also chases squirrels
Do they prefer men or women?: I live alone. she has not been around men in my presence.
Live with another dog? yes and they get along very well after the introduction time.
Been around another dog?: She enjoys the company of the other dog in the house. They get along very well. Play in the backyard together. Will sometimes sleep together. She has helped calm my other dog who has separation anxiety.
Commands known: Knows 'outside' and go in the house. knows sit and come, sometimes down. Working on stay.
Leash reactive?: She likes to walk. she pulls the leash when first starting, but settles after a few minutes. she knows a leash on sight and gets excited. She would try and chase squirrels. ok with people. I have only walked her once. most of the time we just go in the backyard.
What do you use to walk your foster dog?: leash. She would do very well with a 'gentle lead head collar' after it is on her. which she would need to be calm to put on. I use it with the other dog and it works wonderfully.
Leash walking rating (Scale 1-5): 4
Car riding?:jumpy. I usually crate her.
Baths?: no baths given yet
Energy Level:2
How much exercise does it take to tire them out?: yes, after playing with the other dog, both will lay down quietly for hours
If they don’t get exercise, what happens?: She is very calm except when greeting people.
A perfect day for your foster would include playing with the other dog, chewing on a Kong with treats in it, going in the backyard, keeping me company while I watch TV
Cuddly Level: 1
Favorite toys or games: kong with treats
Tell us a funny story: She and my other dog where just getting to know each other. In the house Leigh would try to kiss Loyal. Loyal wasn't interested in that. Leigh keep trying until we went outside. Then she would run circles around Loyal trying to get her to play.
I love my foster and think he/she is fabulous because She is a great companion to myself and the other dog. She is calm, not destructive to anything in the house. She is fun to watch get treats out of her Kong.
What makes your foster nervous or unhappy?: Petting or trying to touch her overhead.
Foster’s manners: Jumps when greeting. can be mouthy, but not always. Has never gotten into the trash even at night when the trash in within reach. She has never demonstrated any destructive behaviors.
Behavioral issues or quirks: She needs to trust you or lay down before she will let you pet her. She will lay down after sitting when you point to the ground in front of her. She will then roll on her back and let you rub her belly.
Medical Issues: no
Social Media presence: Facebook - 2 Instagram (posts/stories) - 1 Nextdoor - 1 Youtube - 1
I am old. I don't do social media.
Last adoption event your foster went to: she was not spayed yet, so I hadn't taken her
What prevents you from taking your foster to more adoption events: I have only had her 3-4 weeks. She was in h eat most of that time. She is going to get spayed this Thursday.
What gear & materials do you utilize to help get your foster recognized? Adopt Me bandana, Adopt Me harness
When was the last time you took your foster out on the town?: I have not taken her out of town
What prevents you from taking your foster out on the town more often?: I have not gone out of town
What is preventing your foster from being its most adoptable self?: Mouthy, Meeting new people, I am just learning how to market her
How can we help?: Gear (Adopt Me)
What day do you give your foster preventatives?: 9th
Are you interested in adopting your foster pet?:No
Would you be willing to have your foster dog transfer to a rescue partner? What is rescue partner?

Foster Questionnaire 11/10/23
Foster’s Name: Kimberly D Eubank
General Personality: Pretty chill but can get hyper at times (morning wake up). See write up on Adoptable Page
Daily Routine: Breakfast around 7-8am (I scarf my food in 2 minutes). Then relax while Ms. Kimberly works either in her office or in my room. He has access to doggie door so can go into fenced yard whenever he wants. Dinner around 4-5pm. Treats whenever I can get them (loves treats). Bedtime around 8-9pm.
Food:Blue Buffalo kibble and MilkBone Chewable treats
Ideal Family & Home for foster dog: Family with another dog to play with. No toddlers or anyone with unstable balance as he does jump up on you and if you aren't ready he can topple you. Ask me how I know.
Houstrained? (Scale 1-5): 5
Does your foster use a kennel without excessive barking/whining, escape attempts or destruction?: Almost never barks, Only whines really when he wants food in morning or I haven't given him enough attention but it is very short lived.
Where do they sleep at night?: In my sunroom as my dog isn't a nice hostess and does not like him in our bedroom with her.
Do they sleep through the night?: Yes
Kid exposure: No
Cat exposure: No
Do they prefer men or women?: No preference
Live with another dog? Yes

Been around another dog?: Totally tolerant. My dog is a brat to him and he just ignores her, goes around her. He would love a playmate. My old dog, ain't it!

Commands known: Knows sit but chooses when to comply!
Leash reactive?: Not reactive, just a puller in general.
What do you use to walk your foster dog?: no pull harness which helps
Leash walking rating (Scale 1-5): 2
Car riding?:He doesn't love it, gets a bit car sick sometimes but tolerates it.
Baths?: No problems
Energy Level:4
How much exercise does it take to tire them out?: He can zoomie around the yard and few times and that usually chills him out for a while.
If they don’t get exercise, what happens?: He does like to tear things so my nice Serta dog bed has seen better days! So chewing mostly.
A perfect day for your foster would include lots of treats and I think playing with another dog outside.
Cuddly Level: 3
Favorite toys or games: Doesn't really "get" toys. He messes with them a little but not a ton. He doesn't really understand the bring back part of fetch!
Tell us a funny story: I wasn't expecting the eating of the doggie bed. So walking into the room and seeing it disembowled was like... ah, that's how we gonna play, huh?
I love my foster and think he/she is fabulous because So sweet and loveable. And I really appreciate how tolerant he is of my not so tolerant older dog. He just takes her in stride.
What makes your foster nervous or unhappy?: Car is the only thing really that he doesn't "love". Now he would love to be in bed with me I know. but that would start WW3 with my dog but he doesn't fuss when I tell him no.
Foster’s manners: Jumps on people. Mouthy. Can get in trash but nothing big, just pulling out paper not like knocking it over and making a mess. Does eat things, dog bed, toys etc.
Behavioral issues or quirks: Just what is mentioned above.
Medical Issues: Nope
Social Media presence: Facebook - 3 Instagram (posts/stories) - 1 Nextdoor - 1 Youtube - 3
Last adoption event your foster went to:none
What prevents you from taking your foster to more adoption events: Dates / times don't work with my schedule, Manners (i.e. leash manners, mouthy, jumpy)
What gear & materials do you utilize to help get your foster recognized? haven't really started to get him out there since I have been working on his manners
When was the last time you took your foster out on the town?: N/A
What prevents you from taking your foster out on the town more often?: I dont go out of town on personal trips that woudl be dog-friendly
What is preventing your foster from being its most adoptable self?: Mouthy, I don't have time to market them, Jumping
How can we help?: Getting foster out on the town, Training
What day do you give your foster preventatives?: I didn't receive any to give him. And I don't have a landscape shot of him sorry!

From foster family: " I highly encourage your team to not pet him and reward him when he jumps up for attention. I've been around animals my whole life, and this only supports bad habits making it harder for him to be adopted. 

I taught him to sit by holding up a closed fist and he was a quick learner.

Unfortunately,  he became so demanding with attention that today me getting dressed and apart for him for 15 minutes led him to protest with major destruction. He will grab anything he can- clothing, bags, etc and tear up and chew apart despite having chew bone, chew rope, multiple stuffies etc.

Later he was in the crate for about 20 minutes after already going pee, and he peed outside of the crate, was trying to get stuff to chew, again in protest of being left alone. 

I went pee and closed the door to him, within a minute he got something off a table and began tearing things up. It is like a child acting out to get attention.

I had family visiting for this entire time and he is awesome as long as someone is there next to him, but this isn't sustainable....even us eating dinner while he has his dinner at the same time,  right by us, sets him off because he wants our attention. 

If I tried to work on my computer,  he wouldn't sit next to me on the couch, but had to jump on me, sit on me and even tried as I stood.

It's important to be aware of as he is a wonderful dog, but he needs training in addition to dog testing. He was more reserved at first.

The only way I could get him to stop barking if crated for night was letting him out, and sleeping out in our living area - it was fine after that.
 No, there isn't space or option for dog crates in a bedroom or for multiple crates in our condo. It's also very disruptive to sleep with a loud animal, moving constantly,  snoring, barking at noises. Dogs don't have to sleep with people and it's really not healthy. I don't think you should be suggesting that to people as most dogs eventually should settle in their crates.

He has definitely been through some things and hit by humans Unfortunately. I tried to give him extra love.

 Unfortunately, the behaviors became worse at the end vs better. As long as he is being hugged, he is happy as a clam. It's like he needs a support stuffie as a companion. 

He was over all very happy and we tried to make him comfortable-
Given he has many good traits, I hope with some training and dog socializing,  he can find a home. 

Note- I tried to get more Weight on him, but he always waited to see if he got people food first. Zero people food was given and this is important no foster reinforces this behavior.
He also got lots of exercise,  and a ton of cuddling."

Ashley noted she may have some barrier or resource guarding, she put her hand up to the gate while she was eating the treat she left behind and Tango bared her teeth, but that was all.

Yesterday, dropped off enrichment before taking him out. He fixated on the leash but managed to “sit” in his kennel and was easily leashed. Once out of the kennel, he tugged on it for a few minutes and then responded to redirection (“down” or “sit”) + treat + verbal praise! It only took a few reps for him to walk well on the leash the remainder of our time. Continued with intermittent reinforcement of good walking, adding in “find it” (dropping the treat on the floor) to keep it novel and fun. 

 

In the play yard, we worked on “stay” (he’s a fast learner!) but he was mostly interested in affection. At one point when releashing him, he bit the leash but redirected immediately with “eh” + “sit” + treat and he didn’t bite it again. Walking on the trail, he was very easy on leash and enjoyed sniffing around. 

 

I’ve detailed it in above notes but will list specific steps below and “pin” for easy reference. I spoke with his kennel tech, Benji, this past weekend and got an encouraging update yesterday that he’s been implementing and finding the techniques to be effective, which has made taking Spanky out much easier. Grateful for volunteer/staff collaboration and definitely seems to point to consistency being key!

Spanky Training/Handling Tips:

? Drop off enrichment to help him expend some mental energy if possible before taking him out. (Frozen enrichment can be found in the white freezer located in the back sally port)

? Before opening the kennel, show him your treats and ask him to “sit” and then give him a treat when he sits. If he’s excited, it  may take a few asks before he responds. Then use the treat on the other side of the loop trick to get the leash on him.

? Keep treats visible as you walk and throw them on the ground for him to “find it” until you get outside or he shifts his attention to his surroundings 

? If he bites at the leash, continue walking while ignoring the behavior. If you are in a contained area, intersperse dropping the leash in response to any increase in tugging. As soon as there is a slight pause or decrease in intensity, redirect him with “down” and/or “sit” and then give him a treat with verbal praise. Repeat as needed.

? Start walking again, a treat + praise or throwing treat for him to "find it" every few steps 

? If he starts to bite again, correct him by saying “eh” and then reset his behavior with “down” or “sit” followed by treat + praise. Then resume walking 

? Once biting stops, keep him engaged and reinforce good walking with intermittent treats thrown for him to find

? When un/re-leashing, first ask him to “sit” first and then give him a treat.

 

** If you try to pull the leash away from him, he will tug back. If you ignore, drop the leash (he's not a runner), and redirect him with a command, then he will drop the leash to fetch the treat!

 

** Continue asking him to "find it" until he is leading the walk and no longer looking at you. At this point, he'll be easy on leash

 

** Any time you need to adjust/tighten/handle the leash, ask him to do something and reward him right as you do it (this results in him focusing on what you want him to do vs. the leash you're adjusting)

Recommendations:
It is incredibly important to manage Theo’s environment so that he does not get a chance to rehearse the undesirable behaviors. If you see that he has already spotted an other dog approaching, move the other way to gain some distance from the other dog. It’s important to not prompt Theo to perform a cue that he is not ready to perform or has not practice under those circumstances. 

Remember, practice makes perfect. Practice all the suggested behaviors in different situations and environments where Theo is successful. Slowly practice outdoors as Theo’s confidence increases and starts to offer unprompted check-ins. Practice scenarios that you have experienced in the past without the distraction. Work on distance, distraction and duration as three separate levels of difficulty. 

See below a list of activities you can do to help Theo with his reactivity and also to meet strangers.

Confidence:
Sniffing Games
Find it! 

This is a great game to play encouraging your dog to find a treat (or toy if he has a favorite toy). Show your dog a treat or his favorite toy, and then place it out of his sight but easily accessible. Tell him to “Find it!”. Once he finds it praise enthusiastically. You can start to increase the difficulty of the game by turning off the lights, adding more treats, using boxes or even hiding treats in less conventional places like inside of a shoe. The rewards for the dog are multiple- he gets a treat or finds his toy plus a very happy handler. If issuing a toy, be sure to reward his find with some play before starting again. 

When multiple treats or toys are used, this particular game helps to build persistence and trust in the handler. The dog may initially find only 2 out of 3 treats, but he quickly discovers that persistence in searching when you give the “Find it!” cue pays off. He learns to believe you - there really is another one there! 

Freework

Introduction to Freework

Place snuffle mats and licky mats around an rea of your hours and load them with treats, yogurt, peanut butter, etc… Let your dog go in and explore the area while enjoying the amazing treats you set out for him. Don’t give him big pieces, this activity is more about the journey of finding the treats. Try using small crumbs so encourage more sniffing. You can also use your dog’s kibble for this. This game allows your dog to freely go in an area and explore. You can also do the same set-up outdoors to encourage him to sniff in situations where he might want to bark otherwise. 


Scatter Feed
Scatter Feeding Dogs: A Step-by-Step Guide To Our Favourite Calm Enrichment Activity!

Why scatter feeding is beneficial for dogs
Scatter feeding provides a way for Theo to use his nose and calm down. 
You can use the same cue as “Find it!”. Do this in your back yard or even Sniffspots! 

Consent Test
Petting Consent Tests movie

Particing this form of consent testing will help Theo have some predictability when meeting strangers. Knowing that he wont be petted unless requested can be very empowering for dogs. When Theo meets strangers, please encourage your visitors to not do strong eye contact or talk to Theo at least initially. Let Theo do some freework or scatter feet for some minutes while he is adjusting to the presence of the new visitor. 

Communication:
Teach Unprompted Attention/Auto Check-In
Auto Check-In.pdf

I am attaching a handout on how to do this but here is a short course on how to teach it with some demo videos: https://suzanneclothier.com/shop/autocheckin/

This is very similar to the “Look at me” cue with the difference that it’s coming from the inside out where the dog is voluntarily offering attention. 

Puppy Politeness Poker
Practice Puppy Politeness Poker by creating a list of reliable cues Theo will enthusiastically perform. Also create a list of real-life rewards that he will work for (meal time, access to a snuffle mat, opening a door, etc). Utilize those cues to give him explicit permission to access something he wants and change it up every time. This will teach Theo to slow down, listen to your request and work for what he wants. Teaches impulse control, attention and it polishes the communication between you and him. 
You can learn more about this concept by watching this free webinar: https://suzanneclothier.com/member_video_library/puppy-politeness-poker-webinar/

Training:
Teaching Touch
Touch.pdf

Once Theo is able to give a “Touch” when cued in different situations, you can start using this cue during walks when you see that he spots an other dog and want to prevent him from reacting. You might need to use smellier rewards in the beginning. 


Practice Wait
I don’t have a hand-out for wait but it sounds like Theo already knows this behavior and he just need to practice. Start small with baby steps. Take one step at a time to build distance. Once you are able to ask Theo to wait and go to a different room you can start working on duration. Once Theo is able to wait for a longer period of time you can throw in distractions like maybe closing a door and then opening it. The more you practice this, the easier it will be for him once you take it outside and introduce it in the stairs. Remember to start out with baby steps, even through Theo already has mastered “Wait” with distance, duration and distractions in-doors, you still want to start with just one step outdoors. 


Management:
Teach 1-2-3 Treat! 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ui6dWBDdDSc

I wasn’t able to find any great videos of this (I should make my own lol) but basically you condition your dog to expect a treat when they hear the word “three”. If you practice this in-doors with no distractions, you eventually will be abe to do this outdoors. When you see another dog coming then you can perform the pattern that Theo already knows and he will prefer to be next to you waiting for the treat instead of reacting to the other dog. 


Emergency “U” turn
Teaching an Emergency U Turn Portland Dog Training/ Teach an Emergency U-Turn for your Reactive Dog/ Noble Woof Dog Training

Teaching Theo an Emergency “U” turn will help you get out of situations where he is likely to react. By practicing this, you will be able to prevent him from practicing the undesirable behavior. 

Scatter Feed
After Theo has had a lot of practice with the “Find it” cue, you can do a scatter feed during walks when you see there is a dog approaching on the opposite site of the street. Please be mindful that this would be done if you are sure that the other dog is not walking towards you or wont approach you. This is meant as a management technique to prevent him from reacting to an other dog and rehearse the undesirable behavior. 

Touch
Once Theo learns touch, you can also do this to basically step aside and call him over buy asking him to touch. This will allow you to position him an a way where he is not facing the other dog approaching and will buy you some time while the other dog finishes crossing.

I recommend booking an in-person appointment to work on counter conditioning and desensitizing Theo to other dogs during walks and address reactivity issues. Additionally we can work practicing polite greetings with strangers. Please tell us anything you would like us to know about this dog to help us find it an adoptive home. : The Good: 

She is affectionate and just wants to be loved on. Her personality is so cute. If you want a velcro dog to follow you into every room and lick your tears away, Leah Ann is for you! She has great puppy energy, but also tires quickly. A short walk is all she is able to do right now, and she loves to walk. She enjoyed sniffing and just taking breaks to take it all in on our daily walks. She pulls a little on the walk and veers left and right randomly, but mostly because her pace and gate is not consistent. She could easily be a great walker with some practice. After a walk or quick play time she would settle and rest or nap. She is treat and food motivated, adored her lick mat frozen treat, and listens so well with or without treats. She is smart, she figured out how to push her way through our doggy gate quickly. She also would seek out carpet or rugs to get better traction so she wouldn't slip on our wood/tile. Smart girl! She enjoyed snuggling in our lap like a tiny dog and took a few great naps that way. Her only potty accident was the first night when she did not know where our front door was. Once she figured out we take her out the same way to go potty every time, she went to the stairs and gave us the look to let us know she needed to go out and no more accidents. 

She slept in a crate in our bedroom with no issues. She did not potty in the crate or destroy the bed, and she did not even cry in the crate. She LOVES toys and balls and she did not destroy any toys with us. We fed her separately from our dogs and she did well, showed no resource guarding, and was totally fine with me moving her food mid meal. I put her food on an elevated surface and it seemed to help her, bending down to eat with the one front leg looked tough. She was slowly introduced to our similar size Lab and 15lb Pekingese. She was playful and curious around both and enjoyed a quick play with the lab. The little dog did not like her (he is an 8 year old grump) and growled to let her know to back off and she mostly left him alone. She did recheck every so often to see if he had changed his mind about playing, and when he did not want to play she eventually left him alone again. Can confirm dog friendly, little dog friendly, and kid friendly. 

When in public, EVERYONE loves her, and she is the best girl. We took her to The Chattahoochee Works and just lounged outside on Saturday and the kids and adults all loved her. She was so friendly with everyone and enjoyed getting affection and treats. She greeted other dogs well on the leash, was friendly with a loose body and wagging tail with no hackles up or stress signs. She was approached by some reactive dogs who barked and lunged at her and she did not react, kept her cool, wagged and sniffed, and ignored. She allowed small children to pet her and was gentle around them. 

We attended the Kids Growth 5K on Sunday and she again did super well in public. She greeted other dogs like a champ, layed on her bed and let strangers pet her. She was fine with the loud music and hustle and bustle but did get scared when there were drummers right in front of us (who wouldn't, it was loud!). When scared she tried to get away from the loud drumming so we walked away and she was back to being calm and ok. 

 

The Bad: 

She still has puppy energy, so she doesn't know what personal space is. She will jump up to greet you and absolutely lick your face if you let her. I'm fine with it and redirected her but some folks might not be, and she can be quite persistent about licking your face. 

We worked on the counter surfing as well, she was VERY interested in what snacks she could find on our countertops and table and had no problem jumping right up to check it out. 

While playing, she could sometimes get a little mouthy, nipping our feet or hands. These were generally gentle nibbles, but sometimes were harder (never leaving a mark though). Again, it's puppy energy she needs to get out, and she was redirected easily by giving a toy to chew instead. 

Stairs are tricky right now. She can go up and down small amounts of stairs especially if she can see the top or bottom. She went up and down up to 8 stairs with no issue. Inside our townhome, however, she was not comfortable going up or down our carpeted fully straight stairs. We had to carry her up and down as she refused to try. We figured out she will attempt the stairs if she can see a landing, but if it is straight up/down a whole flight with no landing, she is unsure and avoids it. I am confident she could work up to a whole flight of stairs, but she is not there yet. 

 

The Ugly: 

Me, ugly crying having to give her back, logically knowing she will not thrive in my townhome with too many stairs.

Realizing that he was more scared then anything, I cracked the run door open to see if he would approach. As soon as the run door opened and I offered my hand for a sniff, he approached me with a low-wagging tail. I offered him my leash to which he lowered his head and allowed me to put it on. Exited the kennel and walked to the mulch yard. When we got into the mulch yard, I let him roam around (with the leash still on). I sat on the bench and allowed him to approach me if he wanted. I observed that he was heavily panting due to stress. However, he would approach me with a wagging tail and allow me to pet his head and back. We left the mulch yard and went for a walk to the next yard over where he did a fence greeting with Bubba Boy. He seemed excited to meet another dog and I suspect he is dog friendly. We then walked inside and I brought him over to the supervisor desk. He stopped midway to greet two customers in which he offered submissive ears and a tail wag. Once at the desk, he was met by a few kennel techs. While he did show some shyness, he allowed one kennel tech to pet his head. We went back to 200, I placed him back in his kennel and unleashed without incident. Recommend L3-SF and a playgroup assessment.
